stories.headline: Trump orders DOJ probe into Democrats over alleged threats against administration officials
stories.note: Trump is hitting back at Democrats' impeachment and punishment threats by asking the DOJ to treat them as possible crimes.
body: President Trump said Saturday on Truth Social that he has directed the Justice Department to investigate Democratic lawmakers he says are threatening Attorney General Todd Blanche and other officials with impeachment and other punishment.

The move follows Tuesday's midterms, which handed Democrats strong majorities in both the House and Senate. Since then, Reps. Hank Johnson of Georgia and Deborah Ross of North Carolina have both said on Dan Abrams' SiriusXM show that they back impeaching Blanche, with Ross saying Democrats should begin with War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Trump insisted no impeachable acts had been committed. The only Democrat he named was Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, pointing to her October remarks at the University of Chicago about pursuing cases against people who "enabled" Trump and wanting young people to think twice about working for his administration.

Trump also said Democrats are threatening Republican donors with prison over their views. He didn't name any donors, though Reuters reported this week that Democrats plan to investigate major GOP donors and corporations, possibly including donors to the White House ballroom. Trump called the people involved "EXTORTIONISTS" and said the DOJ should look at it as a criminal matter.
Why it matters: Democrats haven't even been sworn in yet, and Trump is already signaling he won't sit back while they line up impeachments and investigations of his team and supporters.

stories.headline: MAGA voters reveal who they want to see lead GOP in 2028
stories.note: Rally-goers say JD Vance and Marco Rubio are ready to carry the Trump agenda forward in 2028.
body: With Democrats set to control Congress after Tuesday's midterms, Trump supporters are already looking ahead to 2028, and Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio kept coming up as their favorites.

Fox News Digital talked with people at a Trump rally in Bangor, Maine, one of the president's last stops before Election Day. Several praised Rubio as no-nonsense and experienced, while others said they liked both men equally. One called them "two very outstanding candidates" to keep the movement going.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis also got mentions, with one attendee floating a Vance-Rubio or Vance-DeSantis ticket. DeSantis noted this week that Florida stayed under GOP control on Tuesday. Sens. Ted Cruz and Josh Hawley have also surfaced in early 2028 chatter.
No major Republican has formally announced a 2028 run yet. Some voters said they want whoever can best fill Trump's shoes, and one simply wished Trump could run again.
Why it matters: Even after a tough midterm, the GOP base has a deep bench it's excited about, and the conversation about who carries the America First agenda forward is already underway.

stories.headline: Democrats’ midterm sweep opens path to bypassing Electoral College by 2028
stories.note: Exposes a Democratic push to sidestep the Electoral College that a conservative legal expert says the Supreme Court should strike down.
body: Democrats now hold the governorship and both legislative chambers in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada, which could revive the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact in time for 2028.

The compact, already passed by 18 states and D.C., has 222 electoral votes pledged and needs 270 to take effect. Adding those four states would bring it to 272, and Arizona could push it to 283 if Democrats win both chambers there. Member states would give their electors to whoever wins the national popular vote.

The nonprofit behind the compact says it has sponsors lined up in all five states and expects bills early in the 2027 sessions. Its senior consultant, Patrick Rosenstiel, said states have the power to choose how they award electors and predicted a national popular vote in 2028.

Election law expert Hans von Spakovsky, a former FEC commissioner, called the plan "unprecedented" and said the Supreme Court would likely reject a compact that changes a core structure of the Constitution. He said Congress would have to approve it and expects the new Democratic Congress would, but non-participating states would have strong grounds to sue.
For the compact to apply in 2028, enough states must join by July 20 of that year, leaving under two years for lawmakers and courts to sort it out. Until then, the Electoral College stays as is.
Why it matters: Republicans now have a clear fight ahead to protect the Electoral College, which gives smaller states a real voice in picking the president.

stories.headline: From 'Red Sprouts' to school board races, DSA's years-long effort to reach children gains momentum
stories.note: Shows the socialist left aiming its message at toddlers and school boards, a strong parents'-rights issue for Republicans.
body: The Democratic Socialists of America has spent years building programs aimed at children, from childcare at its events to school board campaigns, and a parents' group says that effort is picking up steam.

In October, New York City DSA's "Red Sprouts" program trained organizers to provide "resistance-driven childcare" with political storytelling and games. The chapter also runs a family group called Comrades With Kids, which handed out DSA-themed coloring pages at a 2025 event. The national group has planned a "Socialist Sprouts" curriculum, and Cleveland's chapter made a kids' coloring book about its housing agenda.

The push goes back at least to 2016, when New York members started a Socialist Sunday School for kids ages 2 to 6. In 2023 the DSA voted to prioritize recruiting school board candidates, and the Los Angeles chapter set up a committee to expand its influence over schools.

The DSA says its childcare programs make organizing easier for working-class families. Alleigh Marré of the American Parents Coalition called the youth focus "insidious" and said it's about instilling one ideology rather than teaching kids how to think. Her group is giving parents tools to spot political activism in schools.

DSA-backed candidates won congressional, legislative and school board races in the midterms, and DSA-backed positions prevailed on 23 ballot measures, including one in Washington where voters rejected restoring expanded parental rights in schools.
Why it matters: As socialists gain seats inside the Democratic Party, parents' rights and keeping politics out of classrooms remain a winning issue for Republicans.

stories.headline: New Jersey town reveals staggering $26M theft days after election, sparking backlash
stories.note: A Democrat-run township sat on news of a $26 million theft until after Democrats swept its local election.
body: Cranbury Township, New Jersey, revealed on Friday that about $26 million was stolen through a fraudulent wire transfer, more than five weeks after it happened and three days after Election Day.

Democratic Mayor Lisa Knierim said the Sept. 28 transfer involved money meant to buy property for the township's affordable housing obligations. A local, county, state and federal task force is working to recover it. About $17.3 million has been frozen so far, leaving roughly $8.7 million outside the freeze.

Residents took to the township's Facebook page asking why they weren't told until after the vote. On Tuesday, Democrat Thomas Szczur Jr. beat Republican Carol Haring with about 64% of the vote, keeping Democrats in control of all five committee seats.

Knierim said residents' concerns are legitimate and that the township is moving to tighten financial oversight, including new assistant administrator and assistant CFO positions and possibly hiring an accounting firm. The township hasn't explained the delay in disclosing the theft.
Why it matters: Voters went to the polls without knowing about a massive loss on Democrats' watch, which fuels distrust in one-party local government.

stories.headline: Republican state lawmakers reported Omar to the IRS in 2019
stories.note: Newly surfaced letters put Ilhan Omar's 2014 and 2015 joint tax filings back in the spotlight.
body: In an exclusive, Fox News Digital obtained an August 2019 letter in which ten Minnesota Republican state lawmakers asked the IRS to take a detailed second look at Rep. Ilhan Omar's 2014 and 2015 tax filings.

The request followed a June 2019 state campaign finance board report indicating Omar filed joint returns in those years with Ahmed Hirsi while legally married to another man, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. The board also ordered her to repay her campaign $1,500 tied to an accounting firm's review of those returns, plus some travel costs.

Former state Rep. Steve Drazkowski, who led the effort, said neither the IRS nor Minnesota's Department of Revenue ever responded. Omar's lawyer told the board at the time there was a tax issue that "needed to be corrected" regardless of her candidacy.

Omar did not respond to Fox News Digital. Back in 2019, she said she was glad the board's process was over but didn't address the joint tax return findings. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said last month a federal immigration and marriage fraud probe involving Omar was referred to the DOJ.
Why it matters: Questions about Omar's past filings that went unanswered for years are getting fresh attention as a federal investigation moves forward.

stories.headline: Melania Trump secures $7.2M for foster care scholarships at LSU ahead of Alabama showdown
stories.note: The first lady landed $7.2 million for foster youth and got 'USA' chants at Tiger Stadium.
body: First lady Melania Trump announced a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at LSU on Saturday for students who grew up in foster care, part of her Fostering the Future initiative.

The fund includes $5 million from MMR Group, led by LSU alum James "Pepper" Rutland, plus $2.2 million from 75 LSU Foundation donors. LSU's president said the lead gift should produce about $200,000 a year for tuition, books, housing and fees.

She told the crowd the scholarships will give foster youth "an anchor of stability" and a chance at a great life. She said 26 universities now support 100 Fostering the Future scholars this semester, with LSU at 14 versus Alabama's nine.

The celebration carried into the LSU-Alabama game at Tiger Stadium, with Fostering the Future patches and decals on uniforms, an on-field check presentation, a military flyover and "USA" chants as she appeared on the big screen. Gov. Jeff Landry and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise were there.
Why it matters: It's a feel-good, bipartisan-friendly win that shows the Trump White House delivering real help for kids who need it most.
